content.text: Read README.md and say in one short sentence what this project is.

availableCommands.name: activitykit
availableCommands.description: Implement, review, or improve Live Activities and Dynamic Island experiences in iOS apps using ActivityKit. Use when building real-time updating widgets for the Lock Screen and Dynamic Island — delivery tracking, sports scores, ride-sharing status, workout timers, media playback, or any time-sensitive information that updates in real time. Also use when working with ActivityKit, ActivityAttributes, Activity lifecycle (request/update/end), Dynamic Island layouts (compact/minimal/expanded), push-to-update Live Activities, or Lock Screen live widgets. (user)

availableCommands.name: alex-writing-voice
availableCommands.description: Alex's writing voice for anything a reader will see in his name — blog posts for alexecollins.com, LinkedIn and social updates, READMEs, App Store listing copy, release notes, talk abstracts, emails and PR descriptions written as him, and every word inside his apps: the first-run "How it works" sheet, permission priming views, empty states, purpose strings, error lines, settings labels and TestFlight "What to Test" notes. Covers how he actually writes (cut hedging rather than soften it, plainer verbs, split long sentences, active voice with the agent named, say why and not just what, warmer over corporate, no paired adjectives), a set of contrastive generic-vs-Alex rewrites, and hard bans on AI-slop words, phrases, openers, and em dashes. Use whenever drafting or editing prose that goes out under Alex's name, and when reviewing a draft that already exists. (user)

availableCommands.name: app-naming
availableCommands.description: Settle an app's final name before it goes to App Store review, on the understanding that most of Alex's apps carry a working title. Covers what the App Store actually requires (a 30-character name, a 30-character subtitle that adds rather than repeats, a 100-character keyword field that never repeats either, uniqueness under guideline 2.3.7 and other people's brands under 4.1(c)), how to test whether a name survives being said aloud and searched for, what to check before proposing it, and how to hand Alex two or three real candidates with the case for each rather than a list. Use whenever Alex asks what an app should be called, whether a working title should stay, to check a name is free, to pick a subtitle or keywords, or before any app of his moves to the review phase. (user)

availableCommands.name: app-rename
availableCommands.description: Carry out a rename Alex has already decided — change the name on the Home Screen, in the app's own words, in the docs and on the App Store record, without changing the app's identity or losing the data on his phone. Covers what must never move (the bundle id, the App Group, the iCloud container, the on-disk store name), reserving the name in App Store Connect before any archive is built, the full list of places a name is written, what to do with the checkout directory and the GitHub repo, names carrying apostrophes and question marks, what to do when he changes his mind, and how to verify it landed. Use whenever Alex says to rename an app, "call it X now", "go ahead with the new name", "Unsocial becomes Fingerpost", when a naming row is marked settled and the rename row comes up, or when a session finds an app whose display name and directory disagree and wonders whether to tidy it. (user)

availableCommands.name: app-store-review
availableCommands.description: Audits App Store submission readiness and rejection risk across current review guidelines, PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy and required-reason APIs, privacy labels, ATT, StoreKit payments, metadata, entitlements, widgets, and Live Activities. Use when preparing a submission, responding to rejection, reconciling privacy evidence, or separating upload blockers from cleanup. (user)

availableCommands.name: background-processing
availableCommands.description: Schedule and execute background work on iOS using BGTaskScheduler. Use when registering BGAppRefreshTask for short background fetches, BGProcessingTask for long-running maintenance, BGContinuedProcessingTask (iOS 26+) for foreground-started work that continues in background, background URLSession downloads, or background push notifications. Covers Info.plist configuration, expiration handling, task completion, and debugging with simulated launches. (user)

availableCommands.name: build-with-alex
availableCommands.description: How Alex builds iPhone apps with Claude, from first scaffold to a build on his phone — the project shape he expects, how he gives instructions (dictated, stream-of-consciousness lists that arrive mid-turn), what he values (authenticity over convenience, no system dialogs, no instructional text, prefer silence to a bad sound), how each round ends (verified on the simulator, installed on his iPhone without being asked when there is something for him to feel and otherwise not, committed, reported). Use this whenever Alex starts a new app, asks to scaffold or "build out" an app, sends a list of changes to an existing app of his (Developed, Persephone, StormyNight, HardStop, Actionable, BrushBuddy, CorpSpeak, Bestiary, MeetingBuddy), or says "make it so", "make X bigger/smaller", "remove X", "change the text", "ship it to my phone" — even when he names only one change, because the round has the same shape every time. (user)

availableCommands.name: critic
availableCommands.description: Run Alex's own objections over a session's work before it reaches him, using the rules he has already stated once in writing. Not his taste and not his judgement: only the cheap half, the things he has said no to before, caught before they cost him a review. Covers the house rules a round breaks most often (the first-run sheet and the line it closes on, no instructional text on a working screen, Settings with How it works on top and a Debug-only Developer section at the bottom, units and dates from the device, silence over a bad sound, a name that is taken is not a name, an audit files rather than fixes, reversible work gets done rather than asked about, a report that ends Done or Needs you), each carrying the date and the words it came from, plus assets/critic-scan.sh for the checks a grep can make. Use before reporting a round, before a first-run sheet or a permission primer goes out, before a store listing or an app name is written, before an audit files its findings, and whenever a session is about to say it is done. (user)

availableCommands.name: in-app-help
availableCommands.description: How Alex's apps teach themselves — the first-time user experience (a one-time sheet on first launch, written in Alex's own voice via alex-writing-voice, with the same three sections in every app: the name and what it is, how you use it in a few steps, and why this one, closing on "Private and free forever"; dismissed once, never shown again, and always the "How it works" row at the top of Settings, which every app has even if only its Developer section is visible in Debug builds, so he can re-read it as it is iterated; then the app doing its job with empty states that show the shape of what comes and defaults instead of setup), the house pattern for device permissions (a priming view in the app's own voice before every system alert, saying what the feature does and why it needs the access, one Continue button, asked at the moment of use, with a calm in-place path to Settings when denied), and contextual help (the object explains itself; a single TipKit tip only for the one gesture nobody would find; never instructional text on screen). Use whenever Alex asks about onboarding, first run, first launch, "what does a new user see", priming, permission prompts, "why does it ask for the camera", usage descriptions, what happens when access is denied, in-app help, tips, tutorials, empty states, or when a session is about to add a call that triggers a system permission alert, or to review an app's first-run before it moves to devtest. (user)

availableCommands.name: ios-accessibility
availableCommands.description: Build and audit SwiftUI, UIKit, and AppKit accessibility for VoiceOver, Voice Control, Switch Control, Full Keyboard Access, Dynamic Type, focus restoration, labels/traits/actions, traversal, custom rotors, NSAccessibility, XCTest checks, adaptive system preferences, and App Store accessibility declarations. Use when implementing accessible UI, fixing an accessibility audit, testing assistive-technology behavior, or substantiating App Store Accessibility Nutrition Labels. (user)

availableCommands.name: ios-localization
availableCommands.description: Implement, review, or improve localization and internationalization in iOS/macOS apps — String Catalogs (.xcstrings), generated localizable symbols, stable key naming, LocalizedStringKey, LocalizedStringResource, pluralization, FormatStyle for numbers/dates/measurements, right-to-left layout, Dynamic Type, and locale-aware formatting. Use when adding multi-language support, setting up String Catalogs, enabling generated symbols for compile-time-safe localization keys, handling plural forms, formatting dates/numbers/currencies for different locales, testing localizations, or making UI work correctly in RTL languages like Arabic and Hebrew. (user)

availableCommands.name: luxury-audit
availableCommands.description: Score how luxurious an app feels — cold start, whether it is already doing its job on open, frame rate and scrolling, touch-down responsiveness, blocking modals, gesture fidelity, animation physics, platform integration, haptics and sound, typography, error handling and accessibility — and produce a score per dimension plus a prioritised list of specific fixes with file and line, separating what was verified statically or by measurement from what Alex has to feel on a device. Use whenever he asks how an app feels, whether it feels luxurious or premium or cheap or janky, why it does not feel finished, what friction is left, how it compares to a first-party app, to audit or score or benchmark the feel of an app, or to run this against every app in the challenge. (user)

availableCommands.name: project-lead
availableCommands.description: Run one of Alex's apps as its project lead in Software Factory — register on the project, decide what it does next, spawn engineers to do the work, and escalate straight to Alex when you must. Covers the two-tier shape (Alex directs and answers escalations directly; a lead owns one app; engineers are the lead's own subagents), how to work a project's backlog through the factory's task tools, how to choose the next piece of work, how many engineers may run at once and what that costs the Mac, what a lead decides alone and what it must escalate, and how a lead reports. Use when a session is appointed lead of an app, when a lead is deciding what to work on next, before spawning an engineer, when a lead's work is blocked or needs Alex, and whenever a session asks who owns a decision about one app. (user)

availableCommands.name: push-notifications
availableCommands.description: Implement, review, or debug push notifications in iOS/macOS apps — local notifications, remote (APNs) notifications, rich notifications, notification actions, silent pushes, and notification service/content extensions. Use when working with UNUserNotificationCenter, registering for remote notifications, handling notification payloads, setting up notification categories and actions, creating rich notification content, or debugging notification delivery. Also use when working with alerts, badges, sounds, background pushes, or user notification permissions in Swift apps. (user)

availableCommands.name: sdlc
availableCommands.description: The lifecycle every one of Alex's Apple apps moves through and what each phase permits — dev (agents build and test it themselves: unit tests, the simulator, then his iPhone and iPad, which he leaves available; the UX review and luxury audit run here and the agent fixes major findings itself and logs minor ones in the backlog, with no approval from Alex), devtest (a build is on his device for him to try by hand; only he says when it is ready for other people), test (TestFlight groups; user testing), review (App Store review: the app-store-review compliance checklist, then the card's handover), live. Each app also has a maturity tier (1 published, 2 ready for review, 3 needs a little work, 4 still being built, 5 proof of concept) and a focus line saying what it needs next. All of it lives in the project's .claude/ship-it.yml. Use whenever a session has to decide whether a build may go to TestFlight or App Store Connect, whether to fix or log a review finding, when Alex asks what phase, tier or stage an app is in, says an app is "ready for testers", "ready for me to test", "send it to Apple", "promote it", "it's still a POC", asks which apps have had which reviews, what is left, what to work on next or for a ranked list, starts a new app (it starts in dev, tier 5), or when ship-it or build-with-alex is about to run and the card has no phase. (user)

availableCommands.name: ship-it
availableCommands.description: Ship an Xcode app end to end — land every branch and worktree on main, bump the build number, build and test, install on Alex's devices, archive and upload to App Store Connect, roll the build out to TestFlight testers, tidy up, and report. Use whenever Alex says "ship it", "ship", "release", "cut a build", "push a build", "push to my devices", "install on my iPhone/iPad/Mac", "send it to TestFlight", "upload to App Store Connect", "merge everything and deploy", or "tidy up and release" — even when only one stage is named, because they come as a bundle and the order matters. (user)

availableCommands.name: simulator-testing
availableCommands.description: Claim a simulator from the shared pool, or Alex's one iPhone, one iPad or this Mac, before testing — and release it afterwards, so the sessions he runs in parallel don't contend for hardware, install over each other, drive each other's screens, or leave simulators booted for the rest of the day. Use before booting or driving an iOS Simulator, and before any `devicectl` install or launch on his iPhone or iPad, or relaunching or driving a Mac app on this Mac, for any reason — verifying a round, screenshots, UI tests, `xcodebuild test`, a luxury audit's measurements, ship-it's test and device stages — and whenever he asks what is running on which device, why one is busy, or to clean up what was left over. `build-with-alex`, `luxury-audit` and `ship-it` all call into this where they boot a simulator or install on hardware. (user)

availableCommands.name: storekit
availableCommands.description: Implement, review, or improve in-app purchases and subscriptions using StoreKit 2. Use when building paywalls with SubscriptionStoreView or ProductView, processing transactions with Product and Transaction APIs, verifying entitlements, handling purchase flows (consumable, non-consumable, auto-renewable), implementing offer codes or promotional/win-back/introductory offers, managing subscription status and renewal state, setting up StoreKit testing with configuration files, or integrating Family Sharing, Ask to Buy, refund handling, and billing retry logic. (user)

availableCommands.name: swift-concurrency
availableCommands.description: Resolve Swift concurrency compiler errors, adopt approachable concurrency (SE-0466), and write data-race-safe async code. Use when fixing Sendable conformance errors, actor isolation warnings, or strict concurrency diagnostics; when adopting default MainActor isolation, @concurrent, nonisolated(nonsending), or Task.immediate; when designing actor-based architectures, structured concurrency with TaskGroup, or background work offloading; or when migrating from @preconcurrency to full Swift 6 strict concurrency. (user)

availableCommands.name: swift-testing
availableCommands.description: Writes and migrates Swift Testing framework tests with @Test, @Suite, #expect, #require, confirmation, traits, withKnownIssue, Attachment.record, processExitsWith exit tests and capture lists, Test.cancel, Issue.record warnings/manual failures, XCTest-to-Swift Testing migration, Xcode 27 interoperability modes, XCUITest UI-test boundaries, performance/snapshot boundaries, mocking, async patterns, and test organization. Use when writing tests, converting XCTest assertions such as XCTUnwrap or XCTFail, reviewing advanced Swift Testing API availability, or deciding when to keep XCTest/XCUITest. (user)

availableCommands.name: swiftdata
availableCommands.description: Implement, review, or improve data persistence using SwiftData. Use when defining @Model classes with @Attribute, @Relationship, @Transient, #Unique, or #Index; when querying with @Query, #Predicate, FetchDescriptor, or SortDescriptor; when configuring ModelContainer and ModelContext for SwiftUI or background work with @ModelActor; when planning schema migrations with VersionedSchema and SchemaMigrationPlan; when setting up CloudKit sync with ModelConfiguration; or when coexisting with or migrating from Core Data. (user)

availableCommands.name: swiftui-animation
availableCommands.description: Implement, diagnose, or review SwiftUI motion using explicit and scoped implicit animations, springs, transitions, PhaseAnimator, KeyframeAnimator, matched geometry or navigation zoom, SF Symbol effects, and custom Animation types. Use when views should animate on state changes, insertion, removal, navigation, or multi-step choreography, or when motion must respect Reduce Motion and Swift concurrency. (user)

availableCommands.name: swiftui-gestures
availableCommands.description: Implement, review, or improve SwiftUI gesture handling. Use when adding tap, long press, drag, magnify, or rotate gestures, composing gestures with simultaneously/sequenced/exclusively, managing transient state with @GestureState, resolving parent/child gesture conflicts with highPriorityGesture or simultaneousGesture, building custom Gesture protocol conformances, or migrating from deprecated MagnificationGesture to MagnifyGesture or using the newer RotateGesture. (user)

availableCommands.name: swiftui-layout-components
availableCommands.description: Build SwiftUI layouts using stacks, grids, lists, scroll views, forms, and controls. Covers VStack/HStack/ZStack, LazyVGrid/LazyHGrid, List with sections and swipe actions, ScrollView with ScrollPosition and scroll-driven reveal surfaces, Form with validation, Toggle/Picker/Slider, .searchable, and overlay patterns. Use when building data-driven layouts, collection views, paged detail reveals, settings screens, search interfaces, or transient overlay UI. (user)

availableCommands.name: swiftui-liquid-glass
availableCommands.description: Implement, review, or improve SwiftUI Liquid Glass effects for iOS 26+. Covers glassEffect modifier, GlassEffectContainer, glass button styles, glass toolbar/tab bar, static status badges vs interactive controls, morphing transitions, tinting, interactive glass, ToolbarSpacer, scrollEdgeEffectStyle, backgroundExtensionEffect, and availability gating. Use when asked about Liquid Glass, glass buttons, glassEffect, GlassEffectTransition, glassEffectID, glassEffectUnion, scroll edge effects, or adopting iOS 26 design. (user)

availableCommands.name: swiftui-navigation
availableCommands.description: Implement SwiftUI navigation patterns including NavigationStack, NavigationSplitView, sheet presentation, tab-based navigation, and deep linking. Use when building push navigation, programmatic routing, multi-column layouts, modal sheets, tab bars, universal links, or custom URL scheme handling. (user)

availableCommands.name: swiftui-patterns
availableCommands.description: Builds and reviews SwiftUI views with modern MV architecture, state, composition, isolated previews, and migration guidance. Covers @Observable ownership, @State/@Bindable/@Environment wiring, view decomposition, ViewModifiers, environment values, .task loading, iOS 26+ handoffs, Writing Tools, clipboard availability, and performance. Use when structuring SwiftUI state, managing @Observable, composing views, previewing meaningful UI states, or correcting SwiftUI patterns. (user)

availableCommands.name: swiftui-performance
availableCommands.description: Profile, diagnose, and remediate SwiftUI runtime performance using code review, Instruments, and repeatable measurements. Use when a SwiftUI screen renders slowly, scrolling or animations hitch, view bodies update excessively, list identity churns, layout work spikes, or broad Observation dependencies raise CPU cost. Covers evidence-based triage, SwiftUI Instruments lanes, lazy-container guardrails, state lifetime, and before/after verification. (user)

availableCommands.name: swiftui-pro
availableCommands.description: Comprehensively reviews SwiftUI code for best practices on modern APIs, maintainability, and performance. Use when reading, writing, or reviewing SwiftUI projects. (user)

availableCommands.name: task-board
availableCommands.description: File, rank and dispatch work for Alex's apps through Software Factory. Alex is the product manager and the tester; you decide the order, file it, dispatch it and report. Covers filing a dictated request into one factory task per decision, choosing where it lands in the backlog, keeping one agent per project, blocking a task on a decision/task/person/other so the factory clears it itself, raising an escalation instead of guessing, and knowing when a session has actually finished. Use whenever Alex asks for a change, a fix or a feature in one of his apps, reports a bug, says "add that to the list", "what's next", "what's waiting on me", "keep going", or when a session finishes and the next task should go out. (user)

availableCommands.name: ux-review
availableCommands.description: Review whether an app's interface can be seen and used by a hand — colour used consistently between controls and never for two meanings, every control at least a 44-point hit region with space around it, controls kept clear of screen edges, the home indicator, the Dynamic Island and the swipe-back edge, sizes and styles that make the primary action obvious and the rest a coherent set, layouts that survive the largest Dynamic Type and every size class, a designed vocabulary of sound and haptics where each physical event has one pattern and the same event always feels the same, sounds are real or absent, and nothing stops the person's music, and every unit, date, time and number following the device's Language & Region settings rather than an assumed country — scored per dimension against the Human Interface Guidelines with a prioritised fix list naming file and line, and a short list of what to check by hand. Use whenever Alex asks to review the UX or UI, whether the controls are consistent, whether something is too small or too close to the edge or hard to tap, whether the colours match, whether the haptics or sounds are right or consistent or cheap, whether it shows miles or kilometres or the right date order or assumes he is in the UK, whether it follows the HIG, to audit the interface, or before sdlc moves an app from dev to devtest, where this review runs in full and the agent fixes the major findings itself. luxury-audit scores how it feels in time; this scores how it looks and whether fingers can use it. (user)

availableCommands.name: widgetkit
availableCommands.description: Implement, review, or improve WidgetKit widgets and controls. Use when building Home Screen, Lock Screen, StandBy, or CarPlay widgets with timeline providers; configurable widgets with AppIntentTimelineProvider; interactive widgets or Control Center controls with Button/Toggle wiring; WidgetKit push reloads, refresh budgets, deep links, Smart Stack relevance, Liquid Glass/accented rendering, widget extension setup, WidgetBundle, App Groups, and entitlements. (user)

availableCommands.name: deep-research
availableCommands.description: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. (dynamic workflow)

availableCommands.name: design
availableCommands.description: Grant or revoke Claude agent access to your Design projects

availableCommands.name: design-sync
availableCommands.description: Push a React design system to claude.ai/design. This runs a converter that bundles the real component code (from Storybook or a bare package) and uploads it. Use when the user runs /design-sync or says "sync my design system to Claude Design".

availableCommands.name: dataviz
availableCommands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

availableCommands.name: update-config
availableCommands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

availableCommands.name: verify
availableCommands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

availableCommands.name: debug
availableCommands.description: Enable debug logging for this session and help diagnose issues

availableCommands.name: code-review
availableCommands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

availableCommands.name: simplify
availableCommands.description: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

availableCommands.name: batch
availableCommands.description: Research and plan a large-scale change, then execute it in parallel across 5–30 isolated worktree agents that each open a PR.

availableCommands.name: fewer-permission-prompts
availableCommands.description: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.

availableCommands.name: doctor
availableCommands.description: Health-check the user's Claude Code setup and fix issues: diagnose installation health — what the `claude doctor` terminal diagnostics cover — from local data (duplicate or leftover installs, PATH, unparseable settings files, broken or colliding agent definitions, skills whose frontmatter fails to parse); find unused skills, MCP servers, and plugins versus their context cost and disable dead weight; deduplicate local CLAUDE.md files against checked-in ones; trim checked-in CLAUDE.md files by cutting content a session could derive from the codebase (directory layouts, tech-stack lists, architecture overviews) while keeping gotchas, rationale, and non-standard conventions; migrate always-loaded CLAUDE.md guidance into lazy skills and nested CLAUDE.md files; flag slow hooks and context-heavy extensions; check the installed version is current; make auto mode the default permission mode; and pre-approve frequently denied read-only commands. Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

availableCommands.name: loop
availableCommands.description: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace.

availableCommands.name: schedule
availableCommands.description: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule.

availableCommands.name: claude-api
availableCommands.description:
Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).

availableCommands.name: workflow-authoring
availableCommands.description: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.

availableCommands.name: run
availableCommands.description: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

availableCommands.name: run-skill-generator
availableCommands.description: Author or improve the run-<unit> skill - a per-project skill that tells agents how to build, launch, and drive this project's app. Use when the user asks to set up the project, get it running, write run instructions, or verify build/run steps work from a clean environment.

availableCommands.name: alex-writing-voice
availableCommands.description: Alex's writing voice for anything a reader will see in his name — blog posts for alexecollins.com, LinkedIn and social updates, READMEs, App Store listing copy, release notes, talk abstracts, emails and PR descriptions written as him, and every word inside his apps: the first-run "How it works" sheet, permission priming views, empty states, purpose strings, error lines, settings labels and TestFlight "What to Test" notes. Covers how he actually writes (cut hedging rather than soften it, plainer verbs, split long sentences, active voice with the agent named, say why and not just what, warmer over corporate, no paired adjectives), a set of contrastive generic-vs-Alex rewrites, and hard bans on AI-slop words, phrases, openers, and em dashes. Use whenever drafting or editing prose that goes out under Alex's name, and when reviewing a draft that already exists. (user)

availableCommands.name: app-naming
availableCommands.description: Settle an app's final name before it goes to App Store review, on the understanding that most of Alex's apps carry a working title. Covers what the App Store actually requires (a 30-character name, a 30-character subtitle that adds rather than repeats, a 100-character keyword field that never repeats either, uniqueness under guideline 2.3.7 and other people's brands under 4.1(c)), how to test whether a name survives being said aloud and searched for, what to check before proposing it, and how to hand Alex two or three real candidates with the case for each rather than a list. Use whenever Alex asks what an app should be called, whether a working title should stay, to check a name is free, to pick a subtitle or keywords, or before any app of his moves to the review phase. (user)

availableCommands.name: app-rename
availableCommands.description: Carry out a rename Alex has already decided — change the name on the Home Screen, in the app's own words, in the docs and on the App Store record, without changing the app's identity or losing the data on his phone. Covers what must never move (the bundle id, the App Group, the iCloud container, the on-disk store name), reserving the name in App Store Connect before any archive is built, the full list of places a name is written, what to do with the checkout directory and the GitHub repo, names carrying apostrophes and question marks, what to do when he changes his mind, and how to verify it landed. Use whenever Alex says to rename an app, "call it X now", "go ahead with the new name", "Unsocial becomes Fingerpost", when a naming row is marked settled and the rename row comes up, or when a session finds an app whose display name and directory disagree and wonders whether to tidy it. (user)

availableCommands.name: app-store-review

Use when preparing a submission, responding to rejection, reconciling privacy evidence, or separating upload blockers from cleanup. (user)

availableCommands.name: background-processing

Covers Info.plist configuration, expiration handling, task completion, and debugging with simulated launches. (user)

availableCommands.name: build-with-alex
availableCommands.description: How Alex builds iPhone apps with Claude, from first scaffold to a build on his phone — the project shape he expects, how he gives instructions (dictated, stream-of-consciousness lists that arrive mid-turn), what he values (authenticity over convenience, no system dialogs, no instructional text, prefer silence to a bad sound), how each round ends (verified on the simulator, installed on his iPhone without being asked when there is something for him to feel and otherwise not, committed, reported). Use this whenever Alex starts a new app, asks to scaffold or "build out" an app, sends a list of changes to an existing app of his (Developed, Persephone, StormyNight, HardStop, Actionable, BrushBuddy, CorpSpeak, Bestiary, MeetingBuddy), or says "make it so", "make X bigger/smaller", "remove X", "change the text", "ship it to my phone" — even when he names only one change, because the round has the same shape every time. (user)

availableCommands.name: critic
availableCommands.description: Run Alex's own objections over a session's work before it reaches him, using the rules he has already stated once in writing. Not his taste and not his judgement: only the cheap half, the things he has said no to before, caught before they cost him a review. Covers the house rules a round breaks most often (the first-run sheet and the line it closes on, no instructional text on a working screen, Settings with How it works on top and a Debug-only Developer section at the bottom, units and dates from the device, silence over a bad sound, a name that is taken is not a name, an audit files rather than fixes, reversible work gets done rather than asked about, a report that ends Done or Needs you), each carrying the date and the words it came from, plus assets/critic-scan.sh for the checks a grep can make. Use before reporting a round, before a first-run sheet or a permission primer goes out, before a store listing or an app name is written, before an audit files its findings, and whenever a session is about to say it is done. (user)

availableCommands.name: in-app-help
availableCommands.description: How Alex's apps teach themselves — the first-time user experience (a one-time sheet on first launch, written in Alex's own voice via alex-writing-voice, with the same three sections in every app: the name and what it is, how you use it in a few steps, and why this one, closing on "Private and free forever"; dismissed once, never shown again, and always the "How it works" row at the top of Settings, which every app has even if only its Developer section is visible in Debug builds, so he can re-read it as it is iterated; then the app doing its job with empty states that show the shape of what comes and defaults instead of setup), the house pattern for device permissions (a priming view in the app's own voice before every system alert, saying what the feature does and why it needs the access, one Continue button, asked at the moment of use, with a calm in-place path to Settings when denied), and contextual help (the object explains itself; a single TipKit tip only for the one gesture nobody would find; never instructional text on screen). Use whenever Alex asks about onboarding, first run, first launch, "what does a new user see", priming, permission prompts, "why does it ask for the camera", usage descriptions, what happens when access is denied, in-app help, tips, tutorials, empty states, or when a session is about to add a call that triggers a system permission alert, or to review an app's first-run before it moves to devtest. (user)

Use whenever he asks how an app feels, whether it feels luxurious or premium or cheap or janky, why it does not feel finished, what friction is left, how it compares to a first-party app, to audit or score or benchmark the feel of an app, or to run this against every app in the challenge. (user)

availableCommands.name: project-lead
availableCommands.description: Run one of Alex's apps as its project lead in Software Factory — register on the project, decide what it does next, spawn engineers to do the work, and escalate straight to Alex when you must. Covers the two-tier shape (Alex directs and answers escalations directly; a lead owns one app; engineers are the lead's own subagents), how to work a project's backlog through the factory's task tools, how to choose the next piece of work, how many engineers may run at once and what that costs the Mac, what a lead decides alone and what it must escalate, and how a lead reports. Use when a session is appointed lead of an app, when a lead is deciding what to work on next, before spawning an engineer, when a lead's work is blocked or needs Alex, and whenever a session asks who owns a decision about one app. (user)

availableCommands.name: sdlc
availableCommands.description: The lifecycle every one of Alex's Apple apps moves through and what each phase permits — dev (agents build and test it themselves: unit tests, the simulator, then his iPhone and iPad, which he leaves available; the UX review and luxury audit run here and the agent fixes major findings itself and logs minor ones in the backlog, with no approval from Alex), devtest (a build is on his device for him to try by hand; only he says when it is ready for other people), test (TestFlight groups; user testing), review (App Store review: the app-store-review compliance checklist, then the card's handover), live. Each app also has a maturity tier (1 published, 2 ready for review, 3 needs a little work, 4 still being built, 5 proof of concept) and a focus line saying what it needs next. All of it lives in the project's .claude/ship-it.yml. Use whenever a session has to decide whether a build may go to TestFlight or App Store Connect, whether to fix or log a review finding, when Alex asks what phase, tier or stage an app is in, says an app is "ready for testers", "ready for me to test", "send it to Apple", "promote it", "it's still a POC", asks which apps have had which reviews, what is left, what to work on next or for a ranked list, starts a new app (it starts in dev, tier 5), or when ship-it or build-with-alex is about to run and the card has no phase. (user)

availableCommands.name: ship-it
availableCommands.description: Ship an Xcode app end to end — land every branch and worktree on main, bump the build number, build and test, install on Alex's devices, archive and upload to App Store Connect, roll the build out to TestFlight testers, tidy up, and report. Use whenever Alex says "ship it", "ship", "release", "cut a build", "push a build", "push to my devices", "install on my iPhone/iPad/Mac", "send it to TestFlight", "upload to App Store Connect", "merge everything and deploy", or "tidy up and release" — even when only one stage is named, because they come as a bundle and the order matters. (user)

availableCommands.name: simulator-testing

(user)

Use whenever Alex asks for a change, a fix or a feature in one of his apps, reports a bug, says "add that to the list", "what's next", "what's waiting on me", "keep going", or when a session finishes and the next task should go out. (user)

availableCommands.name: ux-review
availableCommands.description: Review whether an app's interface can be seen and used by a hand — colour used consistently between controls and never for two meanings, every control at least a 44-point hit region with space around it, controls kept clear of screen edges, the home indicator, the Dynamic Island and the swipe-back edge, sizes and styles that make the primary action obvious and the rest a coherent set, layouts that survive the largest Dynamic Type and every size class, a designed vocabulary of sound and haptics where each physical event has one pattern and the same event always feels the same, sounds are real or absent, and nothing stops the person's music, and every unit, date, time and number following the device's Language & Region settings rather than an assumed country — scored per dimension against the Human Interface Guidelines with a prioritised fix list naming file and line, and a short list of what to check by hand. Use whenever Alex asks to review the UX or UI, whether the controls are consistent, whether something is too small or too close to the edge or hard to tap, whether the colours match, whether the haptics or sounds are right or consistent or cheap, whether it shows miles or kilometres or the right date order or assumes he is in the UK, whether it follows the HIG, to audit the interface, or before sdlc moves an app from dev to devtest, where this review runs in full and the agent fixes the major findings itself. luxury-audit scores how it feels in time; this scores how it looks and whether fingers can use it. (user)

availableCommands.name: dataviz
availableCommands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

availableCommands.name: update-config
availableCommands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

availableCommands.name: debug

availableCommands.name: code-review

Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

availableCommands.name: claude-api
availableCommands.description:
Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
